claim: Actinomycetaceae genomes from human cavities are undergoing sizable reductions, including loss of L-histidine and L-tryptophan biosynthesis.
source: We apply phylogenomics and metabolic modeling to detect bacterial species that are evolving by gene loss, with the finding that Actinomycetaceae genomes from human cavities are undergoing sizable reductions, including loss of L-histidine and L-tryptophan biosynthesis.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, supported by phylogenomic and metabolic modeling analyses described in the manuscript.

claim: The dual-substrate phosphoribosyl isomerase A (priA) gene appears to coevolve with the occurrence of trp and his genes.
source: We observe that the dual-substrate phosphoribosyl isomerase A or priA gene, at which these pathways converge, appears to coevolve with the occurrence of trp and his genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: PriA enzymes adapt from bifunctionality in the largest genomes to a monofunctional, yet not necessarily specialized, inefficient form in genomes undergoing reduction.
source: Characterization of a dozen PriA homologs shows that these enzymes adapt from bifunctionality in the largest genomes, to a monofunctional, yet not necessarily specialized, inefficient form in genomes undergoing reduction.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on biochemical characterization of multiple PriA homologs.

claim: Functional changes in PriA are accomplished via mutations resulting from relaxation of purifying selection.
source: These functional changes are accomplished via mutations, which result from relaxation of purifying selection, in residues structurally mapped after sequence and X-ray structural analyses.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this mechanism based on evolutionary and structural analyses.

claim: Gene loss can drive the evolution of substrate specificity from retained enzymes.
source: Our results show how gene loss can drive the evolution of substrate specificity from retained enzymes.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Gene loss has been implicated in rapid bacterial adaptation after experimental evolution.
source: Gene loss has also been implicated in rapid bacterial adaptation after experimental evolution (Hottes et al., 2013), but this process has not yet been confirmed in natural populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Gene loss has not yet been confirmed in natural populations.
source: Gene loss has also been implicated in rapid bacterial adaptation after experimental evolution (Hottes et al., 2013), but this process has not yet been confirmed in natural populations.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Acquisition of new functions due to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) or genetic duplications is broadly documented.
source: Acquisition of new functions due to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) or genetic duplications is broadly documented (Wiedenbeck and Cohan, 2011; Blount et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In genomes undergoing decay, there is a relaxation in selection pressure that increases mutation rates in functioning proteins.
source: First, in genomes that are undergoing decay, there is a relaxation in the selection pressure that increases mutation rates in functioning proteins as these proteins begin to contribute less to cell fitness (Wernegreen and Moran, 1999; McCutcheon and Moran, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteins in genomes undergoing decay display higher-than-normal mutation rates, making in vitro analysis of protein function a challenge.
source: As a result, these proteins display higher-than-normal mutation rates, making in vitro analysis of protein function a challenge (Couñago et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and logical inference from the previous statement.

claim: Most proteins are monofunctional and are rapidly removed from the bacterial genome once they become dispensable due to gene loss.
source: This is because most proteins are monofunctional, and they are rapidly removed from the bacterial genome once they become dispensable due to gene loss.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about protein evolution during genome decay.

claim: Bifunctional enzymes may continue to operate when only one of their associated metabolic pathways becomes dispensable.
source: To overcome this limitation, we propose to use a bifunctional enzyme to study the evolution of substrate specificity after gene loss, as these enzymes may continue to operate when only one of their associated metabolic pathways becomes dispensable.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design.

claim: The phylum Actinobacteria are Gram-positive organisms with high (G+C)-content.
source: The phylum Actinobacteria, Gram-positive organisms with high (G+C)-content, are ubiquitous and show one of the highest levels of bacterial metabolic diversity (Barka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Actinobacteria, supported by citation.

claim: Actinobacteria show one of the highest levels of bacterial metabolic diversity.
source: The phylum Actinobacteria, Gram-positive organisms with high (G+C)-content, are ubiquitous and show one of the highest levels of bacterial metabolic diversity (Barka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses have suggested the occurrence of genome decay within the family Actinomycetaceae.
source: Moreover, within the deep-rooted family Actinomycetaceae, phylogenetic analyses have suggested the occurrence of genome decay (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Many actinobacterial species lack a trpF gene while retaining a copy of the potentially bi-functional priA gene.
source: Furthermore, we have observed that many actinobacterial species lack a trpF gene, while retaining a copy of the potentially bi-functional priA gene.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' analysis.

claim: The PriA enzyme is capable of operating in the L-histidine biosynthesis pathway as HisA and in the L-tryptophan biosynthesis pathway as TrpF.
source: The PriA enzyme is capable of operating in the L-histidine biosynthesis pathway as HisA, while also functioning in the L-tryptophan biosynthesis pathway as TrpF (Noda-García et al., 2013; Verduzco-Castro et al., 2016; Barona-Gómez and Hodgson, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PriA catalyzes the conversion of N-(5'-phosphoribosyl)-anthranilate (PRA) into 1-(O-carboxyphenylamino)-1'-deoxyribulose-5'-phosphate (CdRP) (TrpF or PRA isomerase activity).
source: The product of the priA gene, which is a hisA homolog, catalyzes two analogous isomerizations of structurally similar substrates: (i) the conversion of N-(5'-phosphoribosyl)-anthranilate (PRA) into 1-(O-carboxyphenylamino)-1'-deoxyribulose-5'-phosphate (CdRP) (TrpF or PRA isomerase activity)
evidence: This is stated as a known biochemical function, supported by citation.

claim: PriA catalyzes the conversion of N-[(5-phosphoribosyl) formimino]-5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (ProFAR) into N-[(5-phosphoribulosyl)formimino]-5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (PRFAR) (HisA or ProFAR isomerase activity).
source: and (ii) the conversion of N-[(5-phosphoribosyl) formimino]-5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (ProFAR) into N-[(5-phosphoribulosyl)formimino]-5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (PRFAR) (HisA or ProFAR isomerase activity) (Barona-Gómez and Hodgson, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a known biochemical function, supported by citation.

claim: Evolution of PriA in response to genome dynamics has led to the appearance of the SubHisA and PriB subfamilies, which have different substrate specificities.
source: Moreover, evolution of PriA in response to genome dynamics has lead to the appearance of the SubHisA and PriB subfamilies, which have been shown to have different substrate specificities (Noda-García et al., 2013; Verduzco-Castro et al., 2016) (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: SubHisA and PriB enzyme subfamilies were respectively discovered using phylogenetics in the genera Corynebacterium and Streptomyces.
source: While these enzyme subfamilies were respectively discovered using phylogenetics in the genera Corynebacterium and Streptomyces, no study has ever centered on the metabolic genes associated with priA in the deep-branching organisms belonging to the phylum Actinobacteria, such as those of the family Actinomycetaceae where the transition from HisA into PriA must have taken place (Noda-García et al., 2015; Plach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as previous work, supported by citations.

claim: No study has centered on the metabolic genes associated with priA in deep-branching organisms of the family Actinomycetaceae where the transition from HisA into PriA must have taken place.
source: While these enzyme subfamilies were respectively discovered using phylogenetics in the genera Corynebacterium and Streptomyces, no study has ever centered on the metabolic genes associated with priA in the deep-branching organisms belonging to the phylum Actinobacteria, such as those of the family Actinomycetaceae where the transition from HisA into PriA must have taken place (Noda-García et al., 2015; Plach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge, with citations supporting the evolutionary context.

claim: The family Actinomycetaceae includes many human oral cavity commensal and pathogenic organisms.
source: Here we exploit the intrinsic features of PriA to explore the link between the evolution of enzyme function and gene loss within the family Actinomycetaceae, which includes many human oral cavity commensal and pathogenic organisms (Zhao et al., 2014; Yeung, 1999; Könönen and Wade, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The bacterial family Actinomycetaceae can be classified into four major evolutionary lineages, including two specific for the genus Actinomyces.
source: We classify this bacterial family into four major evolutionary lineages, including two specific for the genus Actinomyces.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phylogenomic analysis.

claim: One lineage of Actinomycetaceae shows extensive gene loss, including his and trp biosynthetic genes.
source: One of these lineages shows extensive gene loss, including his and trp biosynthetic genes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phylogenomic analysis.

claim: Evolutionary patterns correlate with the sub-functionalization of PriA into two new subfamilies named SubHisA2 and SubTrpF.
source: After the loss of constrictions imposed by the retention of biosynthetic pathways, we found that evolutionary patterns correlate with the sub-functionalization, yet not necessarily specialization, of PriA into two new subfamilies, which we named SubHisA2 and SubTrpF.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary and biochemical analyses.

claim: Gene loss can drive functional protein divergence.
source: Our results demonstrate that gene loss can drive functional protein divergence, and provide unprecedented insights into the evolution of enzyme substrate specificity in retained enzymes after gene loss in the bacterial genome.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: 133 representative organisms from 18 families with available genome sequences were selected for phylogenomic analysis.
source: To find evidence of gene loss in deep-branching organisms of the phylum Actinobacteria, specifically within genera belonging to the order Actinomycetales, we selected 133 representative organisms from 18 families with available genome sequences (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: 35 single-copy proteins conserved among all 133 genomes analyzed were used to resolve taxonomic relationships.
source: We then aimed at resolving their taxonomic relationships using 35 single-copy proteins that are conserved among all 133 genomes analyzed (see Materials and methods and Figure 2A – Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: The phylogenetic tree shows several long branches corresponding to the families Actinomycetaceae, Micrococcaceae, Propionibacteriaceae and Coriobacteriaceae, and to the genus Tropheryma.
source: The phylogenetic tree shows several long branches, which correspond to the families Actinomycetaceae, Micrococcaceae, Propionibacteriaceae and Coriobacteriaceae, and to the genus Tropheryma.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All organisms in rapidly evolving lineages trended towards smaller genomes and lower (G+C)-content.
source: As expected, all of the organisms contained in the rapidly evolving lineages trended towards smaller genomes and lower (G+C)-content (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Actinomycetaceae genomes are characterized by particularly broad variances in genome size and (G+C)-content.
source: The Actinomycetaceae genomes were characterized by particularly broad variances in genome size and (G+C)-content, with the variation being most apparent for organisms belonging to the genus Actinomyces.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: A phylogenomic analysis was carried out using genome sequences of 33 organisms from the family Actinomycetaceae.
source: We then carried out a phylogenomic analysis using the genome sequences of 33 organisms from the family Actinomycetaceae (Figure 3 - Figure 3—source data 1), from which 27 are classified as Actinomyces (Zhao et al., 2014; Yeung, 1999), including the model strain A. oris MG-1 sequenced in this study.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: 205 single-copy proteins shared among all 41 organisms (33 Actinomycetaceae + 8 Bifidobacterium) were used for constructing a concatenated phylogenetic tree.
source: We identified a total of 205 single-copy proteins shared among all these 41 organisms, which were used for constructing a concatenated phylogenetic tree by Bayesian (Figure 3; Figure 3—source data 2), and maximum likelihood approaches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: The family Actinomycetaceae separated into four evolutionary lineages contained in three sub-clades.
source: Based in this analysis, the family Actinomycetaceae separated into four evolutionary lineages contained in three sub-clades: Lineage I, which includes A. sp. oral taxon 848 str. F0332 (Org10); lineage II, which includes A. oris MG-1 (Org21); and lineages III and IV, which form a monophyletic group and include A. neuii (Org27) and A. odontolyticus (Org41), respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The four lineages of Actinomycetaceae group depending on their mammalian hosts and human body niches from which they were isolated.
source: Remarkably, these lineages group depending on their mammalian hosts and human body niches from which they were isolated (Figure 3 - Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Lineage II has the highest (G+C)-content (68.32% on average) and the biggest genome size (3.04 Mbp on average).
source: Specifically, as revealed by genome annotation using RAST (Aziz et al., 2008), lineage II, which has the highest (G+C)-content (68.32% on average) and the biggest genome size (3.04 Mbp on average), has the largest number of amino acid biosynthetic pathways (see next section).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genome analysis.

claim: Lineage II has the largest number of amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: Specifically, as revealed by genome annotation using RAST (Aziz et al., 2008), lineage II, which has the highest (G+C)-content (68.32% on average) and the biggest genome size (3.04 Mbp on average), has the largest number of amino acid biosynthetic pathways (see next section).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genome analysis.

claim: Lineage IV shows reduced (G+C)-content (60.66% on average) and genome size (2.19 Mbp on average), as well as less amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: This observation contrasts with the results obtained for lineage IV, which shows reduced (G+C)-content (60.66% on average) and genome size (2.19 Mbp on average), as well as less amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genome analysis.

claim: The genomic differences between lineages II and IV are statistically significant, including the presence or absence of the his and trp biosynthetic genes.
source: Indeed, the genomic differences between lineages II and IV were found to be statistically significant, including the presence or absence of the his and trp biosynthetic genes (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Genome-scale metabolic models were constructed for all 33 organisms comprising the Actinomycetaceae family plus nine outgroup Bifidobacterium species.
source: In order to reduce the risk of overreaching conclusions based only in homology sequence searches, we constructed genome-scale metabolic models of all 33 organisms comprising this family, plus the nine outgroup Bifidobacterium species (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: Flux balance analysis was applied to predict the minimal nutrients required to support growth for each genome.
source: Next, flux balance analysis was applied to predict the minimal nutrients required to support growth for each genome.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: The lineage II models were generally the largest with an average of 1019 gene-associated reactions.
source: The lineage II models were generally the largest with an average of 1019 gene-associated reactions, which is to be expected since the lineage II genomes are also the largest.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: Lineage II models had the fewest predicted essential nutrients with an average of 19 nutrients required.
source: These models also had the fewest predicted essential nutrients with an average of 19 nutrients required.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: Most biosynthetic pathways for essential biomass precursors are complete in the lineage II models.
source: This result indicates that most biosynthetic pathways for essential biomass precursors are complete in the lineage II models.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the metabolic modeling results.

claim: The lineage I and IV models were substantially smaller with an average of 850 and 843 gene-associated reactions, respectively.
source: The lineage I and IV models were substantially smaller with an average of 850 and 843 gene-associated reactions, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: The lineage I models had more required nutrients (25 on average) compared with the lineage IV models (22 on average).
source: Although similar in size, the lineage I models had more required nutrients (25 on average) compared with the lineage IV models (22 on average).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: The lineage III models were the smallest of all, with an average of 817 gene-associated reactions.
source: Finally, the lineage III models were the smallest of all, with an average of 817 gene-associated reactions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: Lineage III models had fewer required nutrients than the lineage I models (23 on average).
source: Surprisingly, these models still had fewer required nutrients than the lineage I models (23 on average).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: The lineage II genomes were the least diverse, with a very large fraction of reactions present in all models.
source: This comparative analysis revealed that the lineage II genomes were the least diverse, with a very large fraction of reactions present in all models, including those for amino acid biosynthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis of metabolic models.

claim: All models across all lineages share a common conserved core of 695 reactions.
source: Interestingly, a comparative analysis of our models found that all models across all lineages share a common conserved core of 695 reactions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis of metabolic models.

claim: 89% of reactions in the conserved core for each lineage are contained in the conserved core across all lineages.
source: When we similarly compute a conserved core for each individual lineage (Figure 4E), we find that the 89% of reactions in the conserved core for each lineage are contained in the conserved core across all lineages.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis of metabolic models.

claim: Lineages I, III and IV are all undergoing the process of gene loss, resulting in a reduction towards a common set of core metabolic pathways.
source: From these modeling results, we clearly see that lineages I, III and IV are all undergoing the process of gene loss, resulting in a reduction towards a common set of core metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the metabolic modeling results.

claim: Models predicted genomes in lineages I, III, and IV (but none from lineage II) that required L-tryptophan and L-histidine as supplemental nutrients.
source: Our models predicted genomes in lineages I, III, and IV (but none from lineage II) that required these amino acids as a supplemental nutrient, indicating the loss of these biosynthetic pathways in these organisms.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: The presence of the priA gene closely tracked with the presence of L-tryptophan and L-histidine biosynthetic pathways in these genomes.
source: We also observed that the presence of the priA gene, which takes part in both L-tryptophan and L-histidine biosynthesis, closely tracked with the presence of these pathways in these genomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Gene losses could have an effect on the evolution of the retained PriA enzymes.
source: This observation suggests that gene losses could have an effect on the evolution of the retained PriA enzymes.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation about priA gene presence.

claim: PriAs from different lineages are grouped in three sub-clades with distinguishable selection pressures operating upon them.
source: Excluding the out-group, our phylogenetic reconstructions show that PriAs from different lineages are grouped in three sub-clades, highlighted in purple, orange, and yellow boxes in Figure 5A, which have distinguishable selection pressures operating upon them.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: PriA coevolves with the presence or absence of the his and trp biosynthetic genes.
source: This analysis also shows that PriA coevolves with the presence or absence of the his and trp biosynthetic genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phylogenetic and gene occurrence analysis.

claim: The dN/dS value of the purple clade (lineage II and Bifidobacterium), which retains the entire set of his and trp genes, is 0.0636, consistent with purifying selection.
source: The purple box denotes a paraphyletic clade that includes PriAs from lineage II, as well as the PriAs from the genus Bifidobacterium used as an out-group. The dN/dS value of this lineage, which retains the entire set of his and trp genes, is 0.0636, consistent with purifying selection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary analysis, with data in Table 1.

claim: The dN/dS values for the orange and yellow clades are 0.0901 and 0.1459, respectively, which is suggestive of relaxation of purifying selection.
source: The orange and yellow boxes denote polyphyletic groups that include PriAs from lineages I, III, and IV. Interestingly, the included taxa within these lineages lost their extant his or trp genes differentially (Figure 4A), and their dN/dS values are 0.0901 and 0.1459, respectively, which is suggestive of relaxation of purifying selection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary analysis, with data in Table 1.

claim: The higher dN/dS values in the yellow clade seem to be due to accumulation of nonsynonymous substitutions that may relate to changes in enzyme specificity.
source: Moreover, the higher dN/dS values in the clade shown in yellow seem to be due to accumulation of nonsynonymous substitutions, in other words, higher values of dN that may relate to changes in enzyme specificity (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the evolutionary analysis.

claim: In H1 (purple box), PriA homologs are conserved as enzymes with dual-substrate specificity, capable of converting both PRA and ProFAR substrates.
source: In H1 (purple box) we assume that PriA homologs are conserved as enzymes with dual-substrate specificity, capable of converting both PRA and ProFAR substrates.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on evolutionary observations.

claim: In H2 (orange box) and H3 (yellow box), the PriA homologs are expected to be monofunctional isomerases, yet not necessarily specialized enzymes.
source: In H2 (orange box) and H3 (yellow box) the PriA homologs are expected to be monofunctional isomerases, yet not necessarily specialized enzymes, capable of converting ProFAR or PRA as substrates, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on evolutionary observations.

claim: Relaxation of purifying selection is associated with H2 and H3 hypothetical scenarios.
source: Moreover, given that relaxation of purifying selection is associated with the latter two hypothetical scenarios, H2 and H3, our model predicts monofunctional, yet not necessarily specialized enzymes capable of supporting growth.
evidence: This is stated as part of the hypothesis based on evolutionary observations.

claim: Mutation of priA in A. oris MG-1 leads to L-tryptophan auxotrophy.
source: Determination of the growth requirements of this strain, termed ΔpriA_Org21, showed that priA mutation leads to L-tryptophan auxotrophy, demonstrating the physiological relevance of PriA in this organism.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genetic deletion experiment.

claim: The ΔpriA mutant of A. oris MG-1 remains prototrophic for L-histidine.
source: Unexpectedly, however, the ΔpriA mutant remains prototrophic for L-histidine, which could not be explained on the basis of current data.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genetic deletion experiment.

claim: The L-histidine prototrophy phenotype of the ΔpriA mutant may be explained by the association between enzyme promiscuity and genome decay.
source: Thus, it is tempting to speculate that this phenotype may find an explanation in the previously reported association between enzyme promiscuity and genome decay (Adams et al., 2014; Price and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as speculation, supported by citations.

claim: PriA homologs from Org15, Org21, and Org22 (H1) were able to rescue growth of both HisA and TrpF deficient E. coli strains.
source: First, in vivo complementation assays using appropriate priA constructs, showed that PriA homologs from Org15, Org21, and Org22 (H1) were able to rescue growth of both HisA and TrpF deficient strains.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the in vivo complementation assays, with data in Table 2.

claim: priA homologs from Org34 and Org36 (H2) complemented the HisA activity and, to a lesser extent, the TrpF activity.
source: Second, priA homologs from Org34 and Org36 (H2) complemented the HisA activity and, to a lesser extent, the TrpF activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the in vivo complementation assays, with data in Table 2.

claim: priA homologs from Org10, Org13, Org39 and Org41 (H3) were able to complement the TrpF activity but not the HisA activity.
source: Third, those priA homologs from Org10, Org13, Org39 and Org41 (H3) were able to complement the TrpF activity but not the HisA activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the in vivo complementation assays, with data in Table 2.

claim: Only five enzymes out of nine were found to be soluble and could be purified as needed.
source: Only five enzymes out of nine were found to be soluble and could be purified as needed, which agrees with the high mutation rate encountered in the previous section.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the protein expression and purification experiments.

claim: Enzymes from Org15, Org21, and Org22 (H1) showed dual-substrate specificity but also poor catalytic efficiencies.
source: First, enzymes from Org15, Org21, and Org22 (H1) showed dual-substrate specificity but also poor catalytic efficiencies, namely, kcat/KMProFAR from 0.01 to 0.1 μM−1s−1 and kcat/KMPRA around 0.01 μM−1s−1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the enzyme kinetics experiments, with data in Table 2 and Figure 6B.

claim: Only ProFAR isomerase activity could be detected in vitro using pure enzyme from Org36 (H2), with a catalytic efficiency of kcat/KMProFAR of 0.002 μM−1s−1.
source: Second, only ProFAR isomerase activity could be detected in vitro using pure enzyme from Org36 (H2), with a catalytic efficiency of kcat/KMProFAR of 0.002 μM−1s−1, but not PRA isomerase activity, as suggested by our highly sensitive in vivo complementation assay.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the enzyme kinetics experiments, with data in Table 2.

claim: PRA isomerase activity as the sole activity present in H3 was confirmed in the enzyme purified from Org42, with a kcat/KMPRA of 0.02 μM−1s−1.
source: Third, PRA isomerase activity as the sole activity present in H3 was confirmed in the enzyme purified from Org42, with a kcat/KMPRA of 0.02 μM−1s−1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the enzyme kinetics experiments, with data in Table 2.

claim: Mutations that accumulate during relaxation of purifying selection affect the turnover (kcat) of PriA enzymes.
source: The obtained enzyme kinetics parameters suggest that mutations that accumulate during relaxation of purifying selection, which make these enzymes difficult to work with, affect the turnover (kcat).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the enzyme kinetics data.

claim: In H1 enzymes, poor turnovers are compensated for by relatively high substrate affinities (KM), mainly for ProFAR.
source: In the case of the H1 enzymes, the poor turnovers are compensated for by relatively high substrate affinities (KM), mainly for ProFAR.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the enzyme kinetics data.

claim: Enzymes belonging to H2 and H3 have poor KM parameters not only for the substrate of the missing activity but also for the substrates they are active against.
source: However, this does not seem to be the case for the enzymes belonging to H2 and H3, which have poor KM parameters not only for the substrate of the missing activity but also for the substrates they are active against, ProFAR and PRA, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the enzyme kinetics data.

claim: PriA homologs from Actinomyces have poor catalytic efficiencies when compared with bona fide PriAs from Bifidobacterium.
source: Therefore, PriA homologs from Actinomyces have poor catalytic efficiencies when compared with bona fide PriAs from its closely related genus Bifidobacterium (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison of enzyme kinetics data.

claim: Enzyme evolution from bifunctionality to monofunctionality under relaxation of purifying selection does not necessarily express itself in the same way as during purifying or positive selection, where specialization and enzyme proficiency come together.
source: This suggests that enzyme evolution from bifunctionality to monofunctionality under relaxation of purifying selection does not necessarily express itself in the same way as recorded during purifying or positive selection, where specialization and enzyme proficiency come together.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the enzyme kinetics data.

claim: The structure of PriA_Org15 (H1) was solved at atomic resolution of 1.05 Å.
source: However, we were only able to crystallize and solve the structure of PriA_Org15 (H1) at atomic resolution of 1.05 Å (PDB: 4 × 2R, Figure 7; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the X-ray crystallography experiments.

claim: Changes of conserved residues from PriA (H1) into SubHisA2 (H2) enzymes include Ile47Leu and Ser79Thr.
source: Changes of conserved residues from PriA (H1) into SubHisA2 (H2) enzymes include Ile47Leu and Ser79Thr.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Previous independent mutation of Ile47 and Ser79 residues in SubHisA from Corynebacterium abolished the PRA isomerase activity of this monofunctional enzyme.
source: Previous independent mutation of these two residues, even into similar amino acids, in SubHisA from Corynebacterium abolished the PRA isomerase activity of this monofunctional enzyme (Noda-García et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SubHisA2_Org36 has a change of Ser79 into Thr79.
source: Analogously, the SubHisA2_Org36 has a change of Ser79 into Thr79 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the sequence analysis.

claim: The methyl group of the threonine residue in SubHisA2_Org36 may affect the contact between PRA and the hydroxyl group, thus abolishing PRA isomerase activity.
source: In this mutation, the methyl group of the threonine residue may affect the contact between PRA and the hydroxyl group common to these residues (Figure 7A), thus abolishing PRA isomerase activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: The estimated binding affinities for ProFAR (−9.5 kcal/mol) and PRA (−9.2 kcal/mol) were obtained after molecular docking for SubHisA2_Org36.
source: This effect agrees with the estimated binding affinities for ProFAR (−9.5 kcal/mol) and PRA (−9.2 kcal/mol) obtained after molecular docking (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the molecular docking simulations.

claim: The energy-minimized docking model of the productively bound PRA in SubHisA2_Org36 indicates that the catalytic residue Asp11 does not interact with the 2′-hydroxyl group from the substrate.
source: The energy-minimized docking model of the productively bound PRA, in agreement with the kinetic parameters from the preceding section, indicates that the catalytic residue Asp11 does not interact with the 2′-hydroxyl group from the substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the molecular docking simulations.

claim: Comparison of PriA (H1) with SubTrpF (H3) revealed the mutations Gly126Cys and Trp139Gly.
source: Comparison of PriA (H1) with SubTrpF (H3) revealed the mutations Gly126Cys and Trp139Gly.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the sequence and structural analysis.

claim: The introduction of the Cys side-chain at position 126 in SubTrpF could influence the positioning of Arg137 with respect to Asp128, obstructing the accommodation of ProFAR.
source: In PriA, Gly126 faces the active site near the catalytic residue Asp128. The introduction of the Cys side-chain in SubTrpF could influence the positioning of Arg137 with respect to Asp128, obstructing the accommodation of ProFAR, as this region interacts with a large phosphosugar moiety that is absent from PRA (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: Trp139 is catalytically important for conversion of ProFAR by PriA.
source: Furthermore, Trp139, which is catalytically important for conversion of ProFAR by PriA, is mutated into several different amino acid residues in SubTrpFs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PriA function.

claim: Trp139 is important for the correct positioning of the catalytic residues present in loop 5, and for substrate binding through stacking interactions.
source: Trp139 is important for the correct positioning of the catalytic residues present in loop 5, and for substrate binding through stacking interactions (Verduzco-Castro et al., 2016; Due et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The indole group of Trp139 in PriAs can form a hydrogen bond with Asp128, stabilizing the knot-like conformation observed during ProFAR binding.
source: Indeed, the indole group of Trp139 in PriAs can form a hydrogen bond with Asp128, stabilizing the knot-like conformation observed during ProFAR binding.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: Mutation of Trp139 in SubTrpF is in agreement with the loss of ProFAR isomerase activity.
source: Thus, mutation of this residue in SubTrpF is in agreement with the loss of ProFAR isomerase activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Arg83 is differentially missing from SubTrpF, and/or the fragment preceding it contains a two-residue insertion.
source: Arg83 is also interesting as it is differentially missing from SubTrpF, and/or the fragment preceding it contains a two-residue insertion (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the sequence analysis.

claim: Arg83 interacts with the second phosphate group of ProFAR, allowing its correct position in the substrate-binding pocket of PriA.
source: Arg83 interacts with the second phosphate group of ProFAR, allowing its correct position in the substrate-binding pocket of PriA.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: Modifications in key residues disfavor the ProFAR binding affinities in SubTrpF.
source: Overall, these modifications in key residues disfavor the ProFAR binding affinities, a result that is in agreement with the enzyme kinetic parameters and the estimated binding affinities for ProFAR (−9.5 kcal/mol) and PRA (−9.7 kcal/mol) obtained after molecular docking (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The distinctive reactions retained in each Actinomyces genome reflect the preservation of some full biosynthetic pathways over others, conferring a capacity to grow on different sets of environmental nutrients.
source: Our results indicated that the distinctive reactions retained in each Actinomyces genome reflect the preservation of some full biosynthetic pathways over others, conferring a capacity to grow on different sets of environmental nutrients.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the metabolic modeling results.

claim: The phylogenetic proximity of functionally diverse Actinomyces genomes speaks to a strong capacity for rapid adaptation to the diverse conditions present in the human body.
source: This result in turn implies an exposure of these genomes to a diverse range of environmental conditions and selection pressures, while the phylogenetic proximity of these functionally diverse genomes speaks to a strong capacity for rapid adaptation to the diverse conditions present in the human body.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the phylogenomic and metabolic modeling results.

claim: The process of gene loss, associated with relaxation of purifying selection, is the key driver of adaptation in Actinomyces.
source: The process of gene loss, associated with relaxation of purifying selection, is the key driver of this adaptation strategy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Metabolic diversity in complex systems as the human microbiome might be characterized after reconstruction of evolutionary trajectories, which may reflect different bacterial functions and ecological sub-niches.
source: Thus, metabolic diversity in complex systems as the human microbiome might be characterized after reconstruction of evolutionary trajectories, which may reflect different bacterial functions and ecological sub-niches.
evidence: This is stated as a broader implication of the study.

claim: The pattern of reaction conservation seen in metabolic modeling analysis exemplifies a likely signature for gene loss, which could be used to identify these phenomena among other genome families.
source: The pattern of reaction conservation seen in our metabolic modeling analysis exemplifies a likely signature for gene loss, which could be used to identify these phenomena among other genome families.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological insight from the study.

claim: In the context of gene loss, enzyme specialization does not necessarily mean catalytic proficiency.
source: Remarkably, in this context, enzyme specialization does not necessarily means catalytic proficiency.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the study.

claim: Multifunctional enzymes may have more than one constraint operating on them, making tracking functional evolution after selection is relaxed during genome decay more readily done than with monofunctional enzymes.
source: Because multifunctional enzymes may have more than one constraint operating on them, tracking functional evolution promptly after selection is relaxed during genome decay might be done more readily than with monofunctional enzymes.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design.

claim: Only partial selection may be released in the retained bifunctional enzyme PriA.
source: As shown here, only partial selection may be released in the retained bifunctional enzyme PriA.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The predicted metabolic phenotypes unveiled by flux balance analysis correlated better with the evolutionary patterns revealed by metabolic gene occurrence and PriA phylogenetic reconstructions than they did with the natural history told by the species tree.
source: Indeed, the predicted metabolic phenotypes unveiled by flux balance analysis did correlate better with the evolutionary patterns revealed by metabolic gene occurrence and PriA phylogenetic reconstructions than they did with the natural history told by the species tree.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: The occurrence of SubHisA2 in Actinomyces, together with the appearance of SubHisA in Corynebacterium, demonstrates that subfunctionalization of PriA leading into HisA-like enzymes has occurred at least twice.
source: The occurrence of SubHisA2 in Actinomyces, together with the appearance of SubHisA in Corynebacterium, demonstrates that subfunctionalization of PriA leading into HisA-like enzymes has occurred at least twice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: SubHisA is the result of positive selection after the acquisition of an entire trp operon by HGT.
source: Whereas SubHisA is the result of positive selection after the acquisition of an entire trp operon by HGT (Noda-García et al., 2013), SubHisA2 responded to the loss of trp genes, and it evolved under relaxation of purifying selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SubHisA2 responded to the loss of trp genes and evolved under relaxation of purifying selection.
source: Whereas SubHisA is the result of positive selection after the acquisition of an entire trp operon by HGT (Noda-García et al., 2013), SubHisA2 responded to the loss of trp genes, and it evolved under relaxation of purifying selection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: SubHisA has drastic mutations in its catalytic active site, which have been shown to be responsible for its inability to catalyze PRA.
source: Consequently, SubHisA has drastic mutations in its catalytic active site, which have been shown to be responsible for its inability to catalyze PRA, whilst SubHisA2 shows some residual PRA isomerase activity, congruent with the observation that its active-site architecture is almost completely conserved.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between SubHisA and SubHisA2.

claim: SubHisA2 shows some residual PRA isomerase activity, congruent with the observation that its active-site architecture is almost completely conserved.
source: Consequently, SubHisA has drastic mutations in its catalytic active site, which have been shown to be responsible for its inability to catalyze PRA, whilst SubHisA2 shows some residual PRA isomerase activity, congruent with the observation that its active-site architecture is almost completely conserved.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the biochemical and structural analysis.

claim: The subfunctionalization of PriA into SubTrpF has been documented only in this study.
source: The subfunctionalization of PriA into SubTrpF, in contrast, has been documented only here.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: The ancestral activity of PriA is ProFAR isomerase.
source: This functional shift had to involve 'non-proficient' enzyme specialization, since the ancestral activity of PriA is ProFAR isomerase (Plach et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The appearance of SubTrpF with substitutions in its catalytic active-site resulted in the elimination of the ancestral ProFAR activity.
source: Thus, the appearance of SubTrpF with substitutions in its catalytic active-site could be discussed based on previous knowledge about PriA. These mutations actually resulted in the elimination of the ancestral ProFAR activity, which is remarkable because the driving force behind this process relates to the relaxation of purifying selection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: A recent study of PriA sequences obtained from a diverse metagenome classified SubTrpF at the transition from HisA into PriA.
source: In agreement, a recent study of PriA sequences obtained from a diverse metagenome, complemented by some of the SubTrpF sequences studied here, classified this enzyme subfamily at the transition from HisA into PriA (Noda-García et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Actinomyces undergoes interspecies recombination with protein functional implications.
source: Since Actinomyces undergoes interspecies recombination with protein functional implications (Do et al., 2008), such a mechanism may provide a means to explain the sequence heterogeneity found in these Actinomyces PriA homologs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Despite the fact that the retained enzymes possess low catalytic activities, they contribute to the maintenance of metabolism, and therefore, to fitness.
source: It also shows that, despite the fact that the retained enzymes possess low catalytic activities, they contribute to the maintenance of metabolism, and therefore, to fitness.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Evolutionary observations backed with metabolic modeling, biochemical and structural data suggest multiple selection types associated with ecological micro-niches, e.g. environmental cues provided by the human body.
source: Taken together, our evolutionary observations backed with metabolic modeling, biochemical and structural data, suggest multiple selection types associated with ecological micro-niches, e.g. environmental cues provided by the human body.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Enzyme subfamilies are the result of processes involving different selection types upon proteins with more than one function.
source: Thus, enzyme subfamilies are the result of processes involving different selection types upon proteins with more than one function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.
